title: Mazda Teams Up with NICA as the Youth Cycling Organization’s First Non-Endemic Partner
content:
Automotive sponsors and partnerships are fairly common in professional cycling, with vehicle brands supporting teams and events around the world. Until just recently, that has not been the case for youth cycling, at least not in the U.S. Just a few months ago, NICA announced an exciting new partnership with Mazda North American Operations, naming Mazda as its Official Automotive and SUV Partner nationwide and the Presenting Sponsor of NICA’s Regional Events.

Until now, NICA has relied on the generous support from industry partners, including lead partners like SRAM/RockShox and Trek, and platinum partners, like Shimano and Specialized. In what many would consider a watershed moment for NICA, Mazda is the first non-endemic partner for the world’s largest — and growing — youth mountain biking association. And this multi-year agreement runs through the end of 2029.

“At NICA, everything we do is in service of youth development — building confidence, community, and a lifelong love of the sport in a positive, welcoming environment for every rider and family. Partners like Mazda, who invest at every level and for years to come, help us grow that community and reach even more young people who deserve a place to belong.“

-Amanda Carey, NICA President

This new partnership began in September, with Mazda signing on as both a lead partner and the presenting sponsor of NICA’s Regional Events. This fall, that included Eastern (Oct. 24-25), Central (Nov. 7-8), and the first Western Regionals (Nov. 14-15). As mentioned in my NICA article last week, I was invited to St. George, Utah, to attend the inaugural Western Regionals, which included road-tripping in a new Mazda CX-50 Meridian Edition (more on this later). I also had the opportunity to chat with folks from NICA and Mazda about their new multi-year agreement.

When I arrived at NICA Western Regionals two weekends ago, the Mazda presence was quite obvious. I was ushered through the parking lot up to a special Mazda owners parking area right up front. A nice perk, and certainly not the kind of treatment that I’m accustomed to. In the expo area, Mazda was set up between SRAM’s massive tractor-trailer rig and the Trek booth.

Mazda had an adventure-ready CX-50 on display for folks to check out and get inside. They were also drawing a crowd with a Trek SuperCaliber giveaway. Outside of the expo area, Mazda had two of its wrapped Trek-Unbroken team cars lining the racecourse.  

Mazda and Cycling

NICA is in the business of getting more kids on bikes, while Mazda is in the business of selling vehicles. To some, it might seem like an unlikely partnership, but Mazda has recently gotten more involved in the cycling world. In fact, Mazda entered into a multi-year partnership with Trek’s off-road race teams in August of this year. That includes the Trek-Unbroken XC and DH teams, the Trek Driftless gravel program, and various Trek events.

With the NICA partnership, Mazda is clearly expanding that involvement to youth cycling. I spoke with Matthew Rhoads, Mazda’s Programs Manager of Retail Digital Marketing, who explained the brand’s interest in youth mountain biking. He said, “As an organization, we identified the cycling community as one that our owners and fans are participating in. Mazda also has an ongoing commitment to youth sports. This partnership with NICA allows us to show up and support both communities.”

Shared Values

Rhoads was quick to point out that Mazda also knows it needs to show up intelligently and authentically. He said, “We want people to recognize that we share their values, like getting kids outdoors and promoting active lifestyles, and we want to lift the NICA organization because they share those values, too.” 

Kate Punderson, NICA’s VP of Development, shared a similar sentiment, saying, “We’re not going to just partner with anybody, especially a non-endemic; the values really need to align. So we did a lot of research around Mazda’s values and who they are as a company, and we found that we’re clearly aligned.”

The partnership is only in its early stages, but it’s already making quite an impression, and Mazda’s booth in the expo and presence out on the course definitely got people talking. NICA’s Kate Punderson told me that “people are so excited for NICA to have been able to develop this partnership; they see it as a whole new door opening. The kids think it’s so cool, too.” She went on to say, “I think there’s a lot of pride there, like the whole community feels proud to have been noticed. It’s validating.”

And while getting the Mazda brand and vehicles noticed is the point, Rhoads made it clear that there’s more to it than that. “If you have a brand come into your space with cool-looking wrapped cars, that’s going to make an impression,” said Rhoads, “but beyond that, we’re not just supporting a few athletes; instead we’re showing up in a way that provides support and actual value to the community.”

Mutual Benefit

Of course, any sponsorship or partnership needs to be mutually beneficial. Mazda is obviously in the business of selling cars, and partnering with NICA strikes me as a pretty smart business decision. It’s one thing to sponsor a professional team, but this partnership has broad reach along with the potential for meaningful impact. According to Rhoads, “Mazda has over 540 dealers and NICA has 33 leagues nationwide, which cover roughly 90 percent of our business. This gives us a platform for our dealers to be involved across the U.S. and provide value to their communities.” 

NICA, on the other hand, is in the business of getting more kids on bikes, and Mazda’s financial support directly supports that mission. Not only are they the presenting sponsor of all three Regional Events for the next three years, but they are joining Trek and SRAM as one of three top-tier lead partners. “Our vision is that every youth in America has access to a thriving cycling community,” said Punderson, “and I think that fits so well with the Mazda ethos, and their support helps us work towards that goal.”

“We use investments from partners like Mazda to ensure we can keep our membership fees as low as possible and keep those barriers to entry down,” said Punderson, “as well as to provide scholarships and support to leagues.” And as we all know, mountain biking isn’t exactly an inexpensive sport, and the support of a brand like Mazda will undoubtedly be very important as NICA continues to expand and provide opportunities for more student-athletes across the country.

My Takeaway

A brand like Mazda could do a lot of things with its marketing dollars, but I’m glad to see them choosing to support youth sports and mountain biking. I think this new partnership shows recognition of the growth and popularity of the NICA program, which has been impressive, to say the least. The numbers are frankly pretty staggering, with 26,000 student-athletes, 16,000+ volunteer coaches, 100+ teams, and 33 leagues and counting across the U.S.

Now, with a non-endemic sponsor like Mazda involved, NICA can continue pursuing its mission of getting more kids on bikes while insulating itself a bit from the volatility of the cycling industry and ensuring a stable future. And as I observed at Western Regionals in St. George, that future looks pretty bright thanks to NICA, its partners, and the growing community of all those involved.

author: Jeremy Benson
